'''''Ardisia crenata''''' is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the primrose family, [[Primulaceae]], that is native to [[East Asia]]. It is known by a variety of names such as '''Christmas berry''', '''coral ardisia''', '''coral bush''', '''coralberry''', '''coralberry tree''', '''hen's-eyes''', and '''spiceberry'''.<ref name="Grin" /><ref>[http://www.hear.org/pier/species/ardisia_crenata.htm "Ardisia crenata"], "[[Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk]]", 1999. Retrieved on 24 November 2012.</ref> ''A. crenata'' is a compact [[shrub]] that reaches {{convert|1|m|ft}}, often with a single stem. [[Leaf|Leaves]] are dark green, thick, glossy, and have tightly waved edges. The [[flower]]s are small, white or reddish, fragrant, and form clusters. The [[fruit]] is a glossy, bright red [[drupe]]. The [[seed]]s are able to germinate under a dense [[Canopy (forest)|canopy]] and are [[Seed dispersal#Dispersal by animals|dispersed]] by [[bird]]s and humans.<ref name="BFNS">{{cite web |url=http://www.bfns.org.au/index.php?c=3&w=19 |title=Coral Berry (''Ardisia crenata'') |work=Shrubs & Scramblers |publisher=Bushland Friendly Nursery Scheme |access-date=2009-03-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040521145232/http://www.bfns.org.au/index.php?c=3&w=19 |archive-date=2004-05-21 }}</ref>

''A. crenata'' was introduced to the United States in the early twentieth century as an ornamental species. It was observed to have [[escaped plant|escaped cultivation]] in 1982 and is now considered an [[invasive species]].<ref>{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20110524020650/http://www.fleppc.org/ID_book/ardisia%20crenata.pdf ''Identification and Biology of Non-Native Plants in Florida's Natural Areas'']}} University of Florida, 1998.</ref>

Preparations made from the root of ''Ardisia crenata'' are used as an ingredient in traditional Chinese medicine.<ref>*[http://libproject.hkbu.edu.hk/was40/detail?lang=en&channelid=1288&searchword=herb_id=D01036 School of Chinese Medicine database]  {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131002031700/http://libproject.hkbu.edu.hk/was40/detail?lang=en&channelid=1288&searchword=herb_id%3DD01036 |date=October 2, 2013}}</ref>

==Description==
Christmas berry is an upright perennial shrub that grows {{convert|1.5|–|6|ft|}} tall. It maintains a densely tufted growth pattern and is often multi-trunked. Christmas berry prefers moist soil and germination can occur from pH 4 to pH 10. It does well in temperatures of 25 °C and above.<ref name="Coral" /> Germination rates are as high as 97.79% after 40 days.<ref name= Sims />  Its leaves are simple, alternate and measure up to 8 inches long. They are waxy and dark green with a crenate margin containing small calluses within the ridges. The leaf tips are acuminate and their petioles are 3–10 mm long. They have a central vein with up to 18 pairs of side veins.<ref name="Queensland">[http://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/03030800-0b07-490a-8d04-0605030c0f01/media/Html/Ardisia_crenata.htm "Coral berry"], "[[Weeds of Australia]]", 2011. Retrieved on 28 November 2012.</ref> Flowers are white or pink with yellow anthers and grow in axillary clusters and are very often covered in multiple black spots. Plants begin to bear fruit two years after sprouting.<ref name="Sims" /> Christmas berry has an abundance of spherical, one-seeded red berries of about 0.25 inches in diameter that remain on the plant throughout the year.<ref name="Identification">Sellers, A., Langeland, K.A., Ferrell, J.A., Meisenberg, M., Walter, J., [http://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/pdffiles/AG/AG28100.pdf "Identification and Control of Coral Ardisia(''Ardisia crenata''): A Potentially Poisonous Plant"], "SS AGR 276", 2007. Retrieved on 24 November 2012.</ref> The berry clusters often droop below the glossy foliage.<ref name="Sims" /> Berries are consumed by birds and, when present, raccoons, and subsequently excreted; seeds can also be distributed by flowing water.<ref name="Sims">Langeland, K.A., Burks, K.C., {{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20110524020650/http://www.fleppc.org/ID_book/ardisia%20crenata.pdf "ARDISIA CRENATA SIMS"]}}, "Identification and Biology of Non-Native Plants in Florida's Natural Areas", 1998. Retrieved on 28 November 2012.</ref><ref name="Queensland" />

While there are indications the plant may be poisonous to livestock, pets and humans, due to cattle deaths in Florida, there is no scientific confirmation of this.<ref name="Identification" />

==Invasiveness==
Christmas berry is an invasive species in the southeastern United States, escaping captivity in wooded areas of Florida in 1982.<ref name="Queensland" /> The invasive cultivar in this region is originally from Japan. Its cultivation as an ornamental has aided its ability to proliferate throughout the understory of mesic hardwoods. It is now naturalized in hardwood hammocks throughout USDA Plant Hardiness Zone 9, particularly in Florida and Texas.<ref name="Sims" /><ref name="Queensland" /> It is classified as a Category I pest by the Florida Exotic Pest Plant Council, meaning that it is interfering with the local plant ecosystem by out-competing native plants and thereby eliminating them, as well as hybridizing with them.<ref name="Fleppc">{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20121010060155/http://www.fleppc.org/list/11list.html "2011 Invasive Plant Species List"]}}, "Florida EPPC's 2011 Invasive Plant Species List", 2011. Retrieved on 29 November 2012.</ref>

Christmas berry is viewed as an environmental weed in Australia, particularly in its rainforests. It has become naturalized in northeastern New South Wales.<ref name="Queensland" /> It has also been naturalized on two islands of Hawaii.<ref name="Sims" />

==Ecological effect==
The dense foliage of Christmas berry shades out native seedlings of the understory by decreasing the amount of light reaching the forest floor by as much as 70%.<ref name="Queensland" /> Its prolific berry yield furthers its ability to form monocultures, as other natives are unable to compete reproductively with the year-long persistence of berries. These monocultures can reach numbers of over 100 plants per square meter.<ref name="Sims" /><ref>Kitajima, Kaoru. Fox, Alison. Sato, Tomatsu. Nagamatsu, Dai. [https://doi.org/10.1007%2Fs10530-005-5839-9 "Cultivar selection prior to introduction may increase invasiveness: evidence from ''Ardisia crenata''"], "Biological Invasions", 2006. Retrieved on 23 November 2012.</ref> When the mature plants from these stands are removed, juvenile seedlings will take over the space they leave behind.<ref name="Coral" /> The diversity of native plant species in the presence of this invasive is greatly diminished through lowered germination rates in the face of the thick cover of Christmas berry.<ref name="Sims" />

==Control==
===Biological===
There has not been a biological control designated for Christmas berry.<ref name="Coral" />

===Chemical===
A 3% solution of [[glyphosate]] or [[triclopyr]] ester, or 4% triclopyr amine, has been shown to be effective in management of Christmas berry.  However, the effect of glyphosate is non-specific, so the effects of the spray on the environment must be monitored. [[2,4-D]] weakness is also exhibited, with even greater susceptibility during seedling or regrowth stages than during maturity. Triclopyr herbicide is most effective at maturity.
<ref name="Coral">[http://plants.ifas.ufl.edu/node/42 "Coral ardisia"], "[[Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants]]", Retrieved on 24 November 2012.</ref> A basal bark application of 18% v/v solution of Remedy or Garlon 4 is an effective suppressant.<ref name="Identification" />

===Cultural===
Thriving ground cover prior to invasion will help slow down seedling colonization.<ref name="Coral" />

===Mechanical===
Mechanical control of Christmas berry is a challenge. Useful methods include hand-pulling in the case of small-scale invasions. This is not a very efficient method due to the difficulty of eliminating all the surrounding berries littering the ground that will soon replace the removed material. Another option is discing, which tills the soil up in hopes of destroying the [[rhizomes]]. This must be carefully administered to prevent harm to the surrounding local flora and ensure that the rhizomes are subdued. Cutting as well as burning prove to be ineffective due to the strongly rhizomatous nature of the plant. If a mechanical method is used to control the plant, the site must be regularly monitored for at least a year in order to ensure elimination of Christmas berry.<ref name="Coral" />

==Medical uses==
The leaves of ''Ardisia crenata'' are being investigated as a remedy to stop asthmatic contractions and spasms. The plant contains a medicinal substance known as FR900359 that could treat several diseases, including [[asthma]],<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Matthey M, Roberts R, Seidinger A, Simon A, Schröder R, Kuschak M, Annala S, König GM, Müller CE, Hall IP, Kostenis E, Fleischmann BK, Wenzel D | title = Targeted inhibition of G(q) signaling induces airway relaxation in mouse models of asthma | journal = Sci Transl Med | volume = 9 | issue = 407 | article-number = eaag2288 | year = 2017 | pmid = 28904224 | doi = 10.1126/scitranslmed.aag2288| s2cid = 5186303 | url = http://eprints.nottingham.ac.uk/46589/1/Matthey1709131.pdf | doi-access = free }}</ref> [[hypertension]],<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Meleka MM, Edwards AJ, Xia J, Dahlen SA, Mohanty I, Medcalf M, Aggarwal S, Moeller KD, Mortensen OV, Osei-Owusu P | title = Anti-hypertensive mechanisms of cyclic depsipeptide inhibitor ligands for G(q/11) class G proteins | journal = Pharmacol Res | volume = 141 | pages = 264–275 | year = 2019 | pmid = 30634050 | pmc = 6417918 | doi = 10.1016/j.phrs.2019.01.012}}</ref> and [[uveal melanoma]].<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Onken MD, Makepeace CM, Kaltenbronn KM, Kanai SM, Todd TD, Wang S, Broekelmann TJ, Rao PK, Cooper JA, Blumer KJ | title = Targeting nucleotide exchange to inhibit constitutively active G protein α subunits in cancer cells | journal = Sci Signal | volume = 11 | issue = 546 | article-number = eaao6852 | year = 2018 | pmid = 30181242 | doi = 10.1126/scisignal.aao6852| pmc = 6279241 }}</ref>

== In Japanese culture ==
The plant is called ''Manryō'' (万両) in Japanese. Because of the red berries and the wordplay of its name it is used during [[Japanese New Year]] for ''[[chabana]]'' decoration, normally along with [[winter jasmine]].<ref name="murasakihanana.link">{{Cite web|url=https://murasakihanana.link/archives/1936|title = 万両 千両 十両の見分け方 和風の自然な庭に似合う植物（12月）です - Hanana tree|date = 17 December 2017}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.543life.com/shun/post20201228.html|title = 千両/万両 せんりょう/まんりょう｜暦生活}}</ref> Other plants used instead because of their similarity are ''[[Sarcandra glabra]]'' and ''[[Ardisia japonica]]''.<ref name="murasakihanana.link"/>
